question: Residents, livestock breeders, farmers and grassroots organisations are protesting and expressing their strong opposition to the construction of a 1 000-acre photovoltaic park, with 141 791 monocrystalline silicon photovoltaic panels, in Kamarina, Preveza.

The proposed site for the location of the photovoltaic park is even visible from the aforementioned monuments of major significance, such as the heroic rock of Zalongos, an historically preserved landmark, and Zongolopoulos’s sculpture-monument commemorating the Souliote heroines, as well as the archaeological park.
Its construction and operation will have an impact on surface and groundwater and cause drastic changes in soil fertility. Accordingly: 1.

What is the Commission's position on the residents' demand to stop the installation of photovoltaic panels, which is harmful to residents, the environment and emblematic historical monuments, as a consequence of the implementation of the ‘Green Deal’, which dictates investments in RES with the sole criterion of increasing the profitability of ‘green business groups’?

What is the Commission's position on the fact that ordinary working-class people will not only feel no benefit from this development, but will be further afflicted by the impasses they are experiencing, including energy poverty and the unacceptable conditions imposed by energy groups, having the European Union directives of the ‘green transition’ itself and energy liberalisation (e.g. Directive (EU) 2019/944) as an ally for their profitability?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.8.2026) The European Green Deal accelerates renewable energy because it serves both citizens and the environment: it reduces greenhouse gas emissions, improves air and environment quality to the benefit of citizens’ health and safety, lowers dependence on imported fossil fuels and strengthens Europe’s energy security.

Renewable energy projects can benefit local communities by creating local jobs, generating municipal revenues and providing direct benefits to nearby residents. The Renewable Energy Directive (RED)1 includes an obligation for Member States to promote public acceptance of renewable energy projects by means of direct and indirect participation of local communities.

In December 2025, the Commission proposed the European Grids Package2 which includes sectorial measures on the authorisation procedures for large scale energy infrastructures and new public participation requirements under RED, including in relation to benefit-sharing. Renewable energy deployment also moderates electricity prices3.

Renewables have very low operating costs and, when they enter the market, their cheaper production is sold before more polluting and expensive power generation means like gas. In Spain, for example, wind and solar growth has reduced the influence of expensive fossil generators on the electricity price by 75% since 20194. This is particularly beneficial for vulnerable and energy poor households.

The assessment and authorisation of individual projects, including their location and possible environmental or cultural heritage impacts, is primarily a competence of the national authorities, in line with EU law on environmental assessment and public participation.
